# Multifamily Apartment Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> Roof repair and replacement for Shreveport-Bossier apartment communities, coordinated around occupied units, tenant notice, and storm claim documentation

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/project-types/multifamily-apartment-roofing

[All Project Types](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/project-types)

## An Occupied Unit Turns a Simple Repair Into a Notice-and-Access Problem

Apartment communities across Shreveport-Bossier range from older garden-style properties with steep-slope shingle roofs to newer mixed low-slope and pitched buildings, and almost all of them share the same operational headache: every roof issue touches an occupied unit, which means tenant notice and access come before the actual repair work can start.

## Notice, Access, and the Paperwork Behind Every Roof Call

A property manager can't send a crew onto a roof over an occupied unit without giving proper notice under the lease, and coordinating that notice across multiple buildings on a multifamily property adds a layer of logistics that a single-tenant commercial building never deals with. We work directly with property management on notice timing and unit access, building our crew schedule around whichever units have already been cleared rather than showing up and hoping residents are available.

Interior access matters just as much when a leak needs tracing from inside a unit. We coordinate those visits through property management's usual notice process rather than treating it as a separate, informal arrangement, since that consistency is what keeps a property in good standing with its residents.

## Mixed Roof Types Across One Property

A lot of apartment communities in this market combine pitched, shingled roofs over individual buildings with flat, low-slope sections over clubhouse, leasing office, or covered parking structures. Each of those roof types ages differently and needs a different inspection approach, and we assess them separately rather than assuming one roof type's condition tells us anything about the other.

Older properties, in particular, sometimes carry roofs that have been reroofed by building rather than all at once over the years, which means a single property can have several different shingle ages and conditions across its footprint. We map that out building by building so property management knows exactly which structures are due for attention next, rather than treating the whole community as one uniform project.

## Storm Damage and the Insurance Claim That Follows

Hail and wind events hit this region regularly, and a damaged multifamily roof usually means an insurance claim process running alongside the actual repair work. We document pre-existing condition and storm damage separately and clearly, since that distinction matters directly to how an adjuster evaluates a claim, and a property that can't show clear before-and-after documentation often ends up with a smaller settlement than the damage actually warrants.

Ice storms add another wrinkle specific to this region. A roof that handled hail fine can still take damage from ice accumulation and the freeze-thaw cycling that follows, and we check for that separately from wind or hail damage since insurance carriers sometimes treat them as distinct causes of loss.

On a standing inspection across a multifamily property, here's what we document:

- Shingle or membrane condition and age by individual building across the property
- Flashing condition at valleys, chimneys, and roof-to-wall transitions on pitched sections
- Low-slope roof condition over clubhouse, leasing office, and covered parking structures
- Storm damage documented separately from pre-existing wear, building by building
- Gutter and downspout condition, since undersized or clogged systems on older properties cause more damage than the roof itself sometimes does
- Interior ceiling staining reported by unit, cross-checked against actual roof condition above

That building-by-building record gives property management a clear roadmap for capital planning, and it gives an insurance claim the documentation it needs to hold up under review.

## Turnover Timing and When Roof Work Actually Fits

Unit turnover between residents is sometimes the easiest window for anything beyond a straightforward repair, since an empty unit removes the access and notice complications entirely. We ask property management about upcoming turnover schedules when a building needs more than a spot repair, since lining up roof work with a vacant unit reduces disruption without asking a current resident to accommodate a crew overhead. Our [insurance documentation support](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/insurance-documentation-support) work on multifamily claims usually runs in parallel with this kind of scheduling conversation.

## Working With Regional and On-Site Management Teams

A lot of apartment communities in this market are managed by a regional company with an on-site team handling day-to-day operations, which means our reporting has to serve two audiences: the on-site manager who needs practical scheduling information and the regional office that's approving capital spend. We structure our documentation to work for both without requiring a separate version for each.

## Common Questions From Apartment Property Managers

### How much notice do residents need before roof work happens over their unit?

That depends on the property's lease terms, but we build our crew schedule around whatever notice period property management has already given, rather than working ahead of it.

### How do you document storm damage for an insurance claim on a multifamily property?

Building by building, with pre-existing wear documented separately from storm-specific damage, since that distinction directly affects how an adjuster evaluates the claim.

### Can roof work be scheduled around unit turnover instead of occupied units?

When the timing allows for it, yes. A vacant unit during turnover removes the access and notice complications entirely, which makes it the easiest window for anything beyond a quick repair.

### Do all buildings on one property need the same roof work at the same time?

Rarely. Buildings are often reroofed individually over the years, so we map condition building by building and let that determine the priority order rather than treating the property as one project.

### How does ice storm damage differ from hail or wind damage on an apartment roof?

Ice accumulation and freeze-thaw cycling can damage flashing and shingles differently than a hail impact does, and we document them separately since insurance carriers sometimes treat them as distinct causes of loss.

## Ready to review the roof scope?

# Warehouse Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> Warehouse roof inspection, repair, and recover work for Shreveport-Bossier storage and light-industrial buildings along the I-20 and I-49 corridors

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/project-types/warehouse-roofing

[All Project Types](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/project-types)

## A Warehouse Roof Fails Quietly Until the Racking Below Tells On It

Warehouse stock across Shreveport and Bossier City skews old. A lot of these buildings have already been re-roofed once, sometimes twice, before the current owner ever took title. As the facilities manager, you're watching more than membrane condition. You're watching what's stacked underneath it, because the real damage from a slow leak almost never shows up on the roof first.

## The Work Order Behind Every Warehouse Leak Call

A warehouse leak call rarely starts with someone looking at the roof. It starts with a stain spreading across a ceiling tile, a maintenance tech noticing a damp corner of the floor, or a tenant calling in about water near their racking. By the time that work order lands on our schedule, the leak has usually been running for weeks, since a low-slope membrane doesn't announce a small puncture the way a shingle roof announces a missing shingle after a storm.

We don't stop at the reported spot. A rooftop penetration that failed over one rack section often has a matching failure nearby that hasn't worked its way through the insulation yet, so every service call includes a look at the surrounding field, beyond the single point of complaint.

## The Mix of Tenants Sitting Under One Roof Deck

Warehouse space in this market carries a wide mix of tenants: regional distribution accounts moving palletized goods through Shreveport-Bossier, parts and materials storage tied to local manufacturing, and increasingly, self-storage-style overflow leased out by the bay. None of that shows up in a roof inspection report, but it drives every decision we make once a leak is confirmed.

A wet ceiling tile over an empty section of floor is an item for the maintenance log. That same water sitting over a tenant's stored product turns into a different conversation fast, one that usually involves the property manager, the tenant's insurance, and a question about how long the roof has actually been letting water through.

## Humidity, Ice, and the Two Ends of the Weather Range

This part of Louisiana holds Gulf humidity for most of the year, and that constant moisture keeps membrane seams wet longer than a drier climate ever would, which accelerates seam failure at exactly the joints that are hardest to inspect from the ground. On the other end of the calendar, Shreveport gets hit with ice storms often enough that we plan around them, and freeze-thaw cycling at parapet flashing and rooftop curb penetrations does real, measurable damage over a roof's service life.

Wind adds a third pressure point. A flat, wide-open warehouse roof concentrates uplift force at the corners and perimeter, zones the field of the roof never has to deal with, and an aging mechanically fastened membrane is usually the first thing to give way there when a front comes through.

A warehouse inspection has to cover more than a walk across the field of the roof. On every visit, this is the ground we cover:

- Ponding locations and how long the water's been sitting, read off the staining pattern
- Membrane condition at each penetration, curb, and pipe boot on the roof
- Fastening at the corners and perimeter on any mechanically attached system
- Parapet flashing and the tie-in points where an addition meets the original roof
- Drain and scupper capacity measured against the building's actual roof area
- Interior ceiling and racking stains that point to a leak the roof hasn't shown yet from above

That record does more than support the current work order. If a storm damages the roof down the road, a documented history of prior condition carries real weight in the insurance conversation that follows, and it's a record we build one visit at a time rather than trying to piece it together after a claim is already filed.

## Patch, Recover, or Tear Off: What the Deck Actually Decides

Owners and property managers want a clean answer on whether to patch a section, recover the whole roof, or go to a full tear-off, and the honest answer turns on what's happening underneath the membrane, not the membrane itself. If the deck is sound and the insulation underneath is still dry, a roof with a handful of active leaks is usually a solid recover candidate. Once wet insulation shows up across a wide stretch of the roof, recover stops being an option, because sealing new membrane over saturated insulation just locks the moisture in and guarantees a repeat call.

Downtime matters just as much as deck condition. A distribution tenant running two shifts can't afford to have a whole bay shut down for an extended tear-off the way a lightly used storage unit could absorb it, so we break the work into sections and keep the roof watertight over areas that aren't currently being worked. Our [roof recover overlay](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/roof-recover-overlay) work is usually the starting point when the deck supports it, because it's the option that keeps the most square footage open while work is underway.

## Working With Property Management Across a Multi-Tenant Building

Most of the warehouse space we work on in Shreveport-Bossier is leased to more than one tenant under a single roof deck, so access and responsibility questions come up before the actual repair does. We coordinate scheduling directly with property management, protect each tenant's stored goods during active work, and put findings in writing clearly enough that nobody has to guess whose lease covers what when a repair bill comes due.

## Answers We Give Shreveport-Bossier Property Managers Most Often

### How often does a warehouse roof around here need an inspection?

We recommend two scheduled inspections a year, and we add a walk-through any time the area takes a hard hit from wind, hail, or ice, since Shreveport sees all three in a normal year and none of them wait for the calendar.

### Can the warehouse keep running while we recover the roof?

Almost always. We stage the work bay by bay so tenants underneath aren't shut down all at once, and any area storing product that can't get wet gets extra protection or gets moved before we start on that section.

### What's the mistake you see property managers make most on these roofs?

Logging a slow leak as low priority because the building still looks fine from the parking lot. By the time a stain reaches the racking or the stored product, the insulation above it has usually been wet for months already.

### Does a standing-seam metal roof hold up better than membrane on a warehouse?

Standing seam sheds ice and wind-driven rain well and resists puncture from foot traffic, but it's harder to repair in one small area without pulling panels on either side of the damage. Membrane can be patched section by section without touching the rest of the roof, which counts for more on a building where a full shutdown isn't an option. Neither system is the automatic right answer, it depends on how the building gets used underneath it.

### Is coating an aging warehouse roof actually worth it?

It can be, if the deck and insulation underneath are dry and sound. A coating buys real years on a roof that's otherwise holding up, but it won't fix wet insulation or a failing deck, and putting one down over either just hides the problem for a while.

## Ready to review the roof scope?

[Request a Roof Assessment](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/contact)

# Black EPDM Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> Black EPDM for Shreveport's legacy manufacturing and warehouse buildings: field-seamed simplicity, recover economics, and where reflectivity doesn't matter

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/epdm-black

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## Where Black EPDM Still Makes Sense on a Shreveport Roof

Black EPDM isn't the default recommendation it was twenty years ago, but it still earns a place on certain roof assets in this market, particularly older manufacturing and warehouse buildings where reflectivity isn't the deciding factor. It's a simpler field seam than TPO, taped rather than hot-air welded, and that simplicity has real value on a roof where a maintenance budget is tight and the building isn't carrying a heavy cooling load off that surface.

## Legacy Manufacturing Buildings and Recover Economics

A fair amount of Shreveport's older commercial building stock is manufacturing space built decades ago, often with minimal rooftop-driven cooling demand because the space below isn't conditioned the same way an office building is. On that kind of roof, the cooling-cost argument for a white membrane doesn't carry the same weight, and black EPDM's lower material cost and simpler seaming make it a defensible recover option over an aging built-up roof.

We still walk the deck and check insulation condition before recommending it. EPDM over wet insulation is the same bad idea as any other membrane over wet insulation; the seaming method doesn't change that math.

## Field Seaming in Humid Conditions

Taped seams handle Ark-La-Tex humidity differently than welded seams do. There's no weld-window discipline the way there is with TPO, but seam prep still matters: the surface has to be clean and properly primed before the tape goes down, and humidity affects how that primer cures. We don't rush that step because a rushed seam prep on a taped membrane fails the same way a rushed weld does, just on a different timeline.

We probe every seam before signing off the job, same as we would on any single-ply install, and the records go in the same file.

## The Reflectivity Tradeoff, Stated Plainly

Black EPDM absorbs more solar heat than a white membrane, full stop. On a conditioned office building or a medical facility where cooling load matters to the tenant, we'd steer toward white EPDM or TPO instead. On an unconditioned warehouse or a manufacturing building where the roof's job is keeping water out rather than managing rooftop unit run time, that tradeoff often doesn't matter enough to pay a premium avoiding it.

- Deck and insulation moisture check before any recover recommendation
- Seam primer application matched to humidity and dew point conditions
- Taped seam inspection and probe before the crew leaves the roof
- Flashing detail at every parapet, curb, and penetration
- Written recommendation on reflectivity tradeoff before the contract is signed

## Wind Uplift on Older Deck Assemblies

A lot of the buildings where black EPDM makes sense also have older deck assemblies, and wind uplift resistance depends as much on the fastening pattern and deck condition as it does on the membrane itself. We test fastener pull-out on these roofs before finalizing an attachment pattern, because an aging deck can hold a fastener differently than a new one, and that changes what pattern actually protects the building during a spring storm line.

Ballasted EPDM is an option on some flat, low-slope buildings with adequate structural capacity, but we check the deck's load rating before recommending ballast rather than assuming it will work.

## What This Means for a Facilities Budget

For an FM weighing a recover option against a full tear-off on an older manufacturing building, black EPDM is usually the lower-cost path if the deck checks out dry. We'll lay out the tradeoff against a TPO recover in the same conversation, because the right answer depends on the building's cooling profile and how the roof gets used day to day, not a blanket preference for one membrane over another.

We also flag when black EPDM isn't the right call, particularly on buildings where a tenant has started conditioning space that wasn't conditioned when the roof went up. That shift changes the reflectivity math even on an otherwise industrial building.

## EPDM on Flat Warehouse Roofs With Minimal Rooftop Equipment

A straightforward warehouse roof with two or three rooftop units and no other equipment clutter is close to the ideal use case for black EPDM. Fewer penetrations means fewer places for a taped seam to go wrong, and a simple deck like that doesn't punish the membrane the way a plant roof loaded with curbs and ductwork would. We see this pattern on distribution buildings off I-20 where the roof's only job is keeping the racked inventory below dry.

Where a warehouse roof starts accumulating equipment over time, whether from a tenant build-out or an HVAC replacement project, we revisit the membrane recommendation rather than assuming the original spec still fits a deck that's changed since the roof went on.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About Black EPDM

### Is black EPDM outdated compared to TPO?

Not outdated, just narrower in where it fits best. On unconditioned or lightly conditioned buildings where cooling load isn't the driver, it remains a reasonable, lower-cost option.

### Does black EPDM shorten a roof's service life compared to white membranes?

Not on its own. Service life depends more on installation quality, deck condition, and maintenance than membrane color, though the added thermal cycling on a black surface is a factor worth weighing on marginal decisions.

### Can an existing black EPDM roof be coated white later?

Yes, that's a common path if cooling costs become a bigger concern after the roof is already installed. We'd inspect seam and membrane condition first to confirm it's a good coating candidate.

### How do taped seams compare to welded seams for long-term reliability?

Both are reliable when installed correctly. Taped seams depend more on surface prep and primer cure conditions, which is why we don't rush that step regardless of humidity.

### Is ballasted EPDM an option for our building?

Only if the structure can carry the additional dead load. We check the deck's rated capacity before recommending it, since not every older building was designed to carry ballast.

# White EPDM Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> White EPDM for Shreveport medical office and administrative buildings: reflectivity to cut rooftop unit run time and tenant comfort complaints

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/epdm-white

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## White EPDM for FMs Trying to Cut Rooftop Unit Run Time

White EPDM gives owners rubber membrane's flexibility and field-seam simplicity with a reflective surface instead of a heat-absorbing one. We spec it most often on medical office buildings along the Ochsner LSU Health corridor and administrative buildings where tenant comfort complaints and rooftop unit run time are both things an FM actually gets measured on.

## Why Reflectivity Shows Up in a Work Order Log

A dark roof surface pushes more heat into the building envelope and makes rooftop units work harder to hold setpoint, especially through a Shreveport summer that sits in the 90s for weeks at a stretch with humidity working against every unit on the roof. When a rooftop unit is already running near its capacity limit on a hot afternoon, that extra thermal load from a dark membrane is often the difference between holding temperature and a tenant comfort call landing on your desk.

White EPDM doesn't eliminate that call volume, but it takes one variable out of the equation, which matters when you're already managing aging rooftop equipment on a deferred replacement schedule.

## Reflectivity Decay and Realistic Expectations

We tell owners upfront that a white membrane's reflectivity is highest on day one and declines from there. Humidity in this region promotes algae and mildew growth on membrane surfaces faster than a drier climate would, and that staining cuts into reflectivity well before the membrane itself is due for replacement. Periodic membrane washing is a maintenance line item worth budgeting for if reflectivity matters enough to justify the white membrane in the first place.

We don't oversell the cooling-cost benefit. It's real, but it's incremental, and a building with undersized or aging rooftop units will still need a mechanical fix regardless of membrane color.

## Field Seaming and Install Timing

Taped seams on white EPDM follow the same discipline as black EPDM: clean surface prep, correct primer application, and attention to humidity and dew point during install. We don't change our seam standard based on membrane color, and every seam gets probed before the crew leaves.

- Rooftop unit inventory and run-time review before recommending a membrane
- Deck and insulation moisture check ahead of any recover decision
- Taped seam prep matched to dew point and surface temperature conditions
- Flashing and curb detail checked penetration by penetration
- Membrane wash-down schedule discussed for reflectivity upkeep

## Medical and Administrative Building Considerations

Medical office buildings carry a different downtime tolerance than a warehouse. Rooftop work above occupied exam rooms or lab space needs sequencing that limits noise and interior disruption, and we plan install schedules around occupied hours rather than treating every roof the same way. On buildings with equipment sensitive to temperature swings, like imaging suites, we coordinate closely with facilities staff before opening any section of the deck.

Tenant notification matters as much as the technical spec on these buildings. We'll give you the language for that notice if you need it, because a surprised tenant calls the building office before they call maintenance, and that call lands on you either way.

## Wind Uplift and Storm Season Fastening

The same spring storm lines that bring hail through this region bring the wind that tests a roof's fastening pattern. White EPDM's attachment method, whether fully adhered, mechanically fastened, or ballasted, gets engineered to the building's wind zone rather than a generic code minimum, because a marginal pattern shows its weakness at the parapet edge during exactly the kind of fast-moving line that comes through here with little warning.

We document fastener spacing and pull-out testing on every install so that record exists if a wind claim comes up years later.

## Reading Building Automation Data Before Recommending a Membrane

Most medical office and administrative buildings in this market run a building automation system that logs rooftop unit run time, and that data tells us more about a roof's real cooling burden than a walk-through ever could. If an FM can pull run-time trends showing units cycling near capacity through the summer, that's a stronger case for white EPDM's reflectivity benefit than a general assumption about the building's age or exposure.

We'll ask for that data before finalizing a membrane recommendation where it's available, because it turns a subjective color preference into a decision backed by the building's own operating history.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About White EPDM

### How much does white EPDM actually reduce cooling costs?

It reduces heat gain through the roof assembly, which helps rooftop units cycle less on hot afternoons, but the size of that benefit depends on insulation levels and unit condition. It's a contributing factor, not a fix for undersized equipment.

### Does the white surface stay white in this climate?

Not indefinitely. Humidity here promotes algae and mildew growth that dulls the surface faster than in a drier region. Periodic washing helps but reflectivity does decline over the membrane's service life.

### Can we install white EPDM over an occupied medical building without shutting down operations?

Usually yes, with sequenced access and clear tenant notice. We plan sections to limit noise near sensitive spaces and keep the deck weathertight at the end of every shift.

### Is white EPDM more expensive than black EPDM?

Slightly, due to the membrane compound, but the cost difference is usually small relative to the total project and worth it on a conditioned building where reflectivity has real value.

### What's the maintenance difference between white and black EPDM?

White membranes benefit more from periodic washing to preserve reflectivity. Beyond that, seam inspection and flashing checks follow the same schedule regardless of color.

# SBS Modified Bitumen Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> SBS modified bitumen for Shreveport's older downtown roof stock: familiar BUR-adjacent chemistry for tie-ins, restoration, and phased re-roofing

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/modified-bitumen-sbs

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## Modified Bitumen for Shreveport's Older Downtown Roof Stock

A good portion of downtown Shreveport's office and commercial building stock still carries a built-up roof somewhere in its history, and SBS modified bitumen is often the most practical path forward on those buildings. It's chemistry that ties into an existing BUR system more naturally than a single-ply membrane does, which matters on phased re-roofing projects where budget or occupancy constraints mean the whole roof doesn't get replaced in one shot.

## Why Tie-In Compatibility Matters on Older Buildings

When a downtown building's roof gets replaced in sections over several budget cycles rather than all at once, the new membrane has to interface cleanly with whatever's staying in place for now. SBS modified bitumen's asphalt-based chemistry bonds to existing BUR flashings and adjacent sections in a way that a TPO or PVC membrane can't without additional transition detailing. On a building where full replacement isn't in this year's capital plan, that compatibility is often the deciding factor.

We map what's staying and what's being replaced before recommending a system, because the tie-in detail is where phased projects succeed or fail, not the field membrane itself.

## Torch-Applied Versus Self-Adhered Installation

SBS modified bitumen installs either torch-applied or self-adhered, and the choice matters more on an occupied downtown building than it does on a vacant warehouse. Torch application requires an active fire watch and coordination with building occupants below, which we plan around office hours and tenant schedules rather than showing up and figuring it out on site. Self-adhered systems avoid the open-flame concern entirely and are often the better fit for occupied buildings with tenants working underneath the roof deck during the project.

We'll lay out both options with their tradeoffs rather than defaulting to one method, because the right choice depends as much on occupancy and fire-watch logistics as it does on the roof assembly itself.

## Multi-Ply Redundancy Against Summer Humidity

Multi-ply modified bitumen systems give a redundancy that single-ply membranes don't have in the same way: if the cap sheet develops a localized issue, the base ply is still there doing its job while repairs get scheduled. That matters through a Shreveport summer where sustained humidity and afternoon thunderstorm activity mean a roof rarely gets a long dry stretch to fully cure a repair before the next rain arrives.

- Assessment of existing BUR sections staying in place versus being replaced
- Torch-applied versus self-adhered decision based on occupancy and fire-watch needs
- Base ply and cap sheet installed with proper overlap at every seam
- Flashing tie-in detailed at every transition to remaining roof sections
- Post-install inspection of laps and seams before the crew demobilizes

## Restoration Economics Over a Full Tear-Off

Not every aging BUR roof downtown needs a full replacement. If the deck is dry and the existing system's structural bones are sound, a modified bitumen cap sheet application over the existing roof, or a targeted section replacement, can extend service life at a fraction of full tear-off cost. We core-cut before making that call, because guessing at deck condition on a downtown building with unknown roofing history is how a restoration budget turns into an emergency tear-off mid-project.

We'd rather deliver a smaller, honest scope this budget cycle than oversell a full replacement the building doesn't need yet.

## Wind Uplift on Older Parapet Details

Downtown buildings often have parapet and coping details that predate current fastening standards, and that's exactly where wind uplift shows up first during a spring storm line. We inspect coping attachment and base flashing condition on every modified bitumen project regardless of whether the scope includes parapet work, because a new field membrane doesn't help if the edge detail lets wind get underneath it.

Where the existing edge metal is undersized or loose, we flag it before the crew leaves, even if repairing it falls outside this project's original scope.

## Material Staging on Downtown Building Sites

Older downtown buildings near Texas Street and the casino corridor often don't have the loading dock or lay-down space a suburban plant roof would offer, and hot mopped or torch-applied modified bitumen needs kettle or torch equipment staged somewhere workable. We scout access, elevator capacity, and street-level staging before quoting a downtown project, because a crew that shows up without a workable material path ends up burning half a shift figuring out logistics that should have been solved in advance.

Parking and loading restrictions downtown also shape scheduling, and we'll coordinate delivery windows with building management rather than assuming a truck can just pull up whenever the material's ready.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About Modified Bitumen

### Does modified bitumen cost less than a single-ply replacement?

Often, yes, particularly for a phased or restoration approach, though a full multi-ply tear-off and replacement can run comparable to single-ply depending on the building.

### Can torch-applied work happen in an occupied downtown building?

Yes, with an active fire watch and coordination around tenant schedules. Self-adhered systems are often preferred on occupied buildings to avoid the open-flame logistics entirely.

### How do we know if our BUR roof is a restoration candidate or needs full replacement?

A core cut tells us whether the deck and insulation are dry. If they are, restoration is often viable; if moisture has already gotten in, replacement is the more honest recommendation.

### Does modified bitumen handle Shreveport's summer humidity well?

Yes, the multi-ply redundancy helps here specifically, since a localized cap sheet issue doesn't immediately become a leak the way a single-ply membrane breach can.

### What's the biggest risk on older parapet details during a mod-bit project?

Undersized or loose edge metal that lets wind get under the membrane at the perimeter, regardless of how well the field membrane itself is installed.

# Modified Bitumen Roofing Systems in Shreveport

> Modified bitumen roofing systems in Shreveport, including SBS and APP options, flashing details, repairs, recover planning, and commercial roof replacement.

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/modified-bitumen-systems

Commercial Roofers of Shreveport

A modified-bitumen decision should begin with the existing roof, not a product preference. Moisture, attachment, flashing height, drainage, insulation, penetrations, and occupied-building limits are documented before repair, recover, or replacement is selected.

[Request a Commercial Roof Review](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/contact)

## SBS and APP system choices

SBS sheets are formulated for flexibility and are commonly installed with hot asphalt, cold adhesive, self-adhered products, or approved heat-welding methods. APP sheets use a different modifier and are often heat welded by trained crews. The assembly and application method must match the substrate, fire-safety plan, manufacturer details, and site restrictions.

## Where modified bitumen fits

The system can be practical on low-slope commercial roofs with frequent service traffic, complex flashing, smaller roof sections, or an existing asphalt-based assembly. Suitability still depends on moisture findings, structural capacity, drainage, insulation targets, and whether tear-off or recover is allowed.

## Repairability and recurring leaks

Repairs should identify the actual entry point and the limits of deteriorated material. Open laps, punctures, failed pitch pockets, wall flashing, drains, and edge conditions are reviewed together. Surface patches alone should not conceal wet insulation or movement below the membrane.

## Recover versus replacement

A recover can reduce disruption when the existing deck and assembly qualify, but it adds weight and can hide trapped moisture or unstable materials. Replacement exposes the deck and supports a complete insulation and drainage correction. Core cuts, moisture investigation, code requirements, and warranty goals guide the choice.

## Installation planning for occupied buildings

Odor, heat, staging, rooftop equipment, pedestrian routes, deliveries, interior sensitivity, and daily dry-in limits belong in the scope. The safest installation method is selected for the actual facility rather than assumed from the membrane name.

## Conditions included in the review

- Deck and existing assembly
- Core cuts and moisture findings
- SBS or APP sheet configuration
- Attachment and application method
- Drainage and tapered insulation
- Flashings, penetrations, edges, and warranty details

## Related commercial roofing services

- [Commercial Roof Leak Repair](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/commercial-roof-leak-repair)
- [Storm Damage Roof Repair](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/storm-damage-roof-repair)
- [Commercial Roof Inspection](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/commercial-roof-inspection)
- [Commercial Reroofing](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/commercial-reroofing)
- [Roof Drains and Scuppers](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/roof-drains-scuppers)

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a modified-bitumen roof?

It is a reinforced asphalt-based membrane system manufactured in sheets, commonly using SBS or APP modifiers and installed as part of a multi-layer commercial roof assembly.

### Can modified bitumen be installed over an existing roof?

Sometimes. The existing assembly, deck, moisture, attachment, number of roof layers, code, weight, drainage, and manufacturer requirements must all support a recover.

### Can a modified-bitumen roof be repaired?

Often, if the defect and wet-material boundaries can be identified and the remaining membrane can accept a compatible repair. Widespread moisture or deterioration can make replacement more defensible.

# PVC Roof Systems in Shreveport, LA

> PVC membrane for Shreveport-Bossier casino kitchen exhaust and restaurant roofs: grease and chemical resistance where TPO and EPDM fall short

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/pvc-roof-systems

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## PVC Membrane for Grease-Heavy Casino and Restaurant Roofs

PVC single-ply is the membrane we reach for when grease and chemical exposure are part of the roof's daily environment, and that describes a specific slice of the Shreveport-Bossier market well: riverboat casino back-of-house kitchen exhaust, standalone restaurant rooftops, and any building venting commercial kitchen equipment across the deck. TPO and EPDM both degrade faster under sustained grease contact than PVC does, and that difference shows up over years of service life, well beyond anything a spec sheet alone would tell you.

## Why Grease Exposure Changes the Membrane Decision

Kitchen exhaust fans push grease-laden air across whatever roof surface sits downwind of them, and over years that residue accumulates on the membrane surface and works into seams if the membrane wasn't built to resist it. On a casino property with multiple kitchen operations feeding rooftop exhaust, that exposure is constant and concentrated in specific zones of the roof, not evenly spread across the whole deck.

We map exhaust discharge points before recommending membrane type, because a building with one small kitchen exhaust vent doesn't need whole-roof PVC, but a property with several commercial kitchens venting across a shared back-of-house roof usually does.

## Hot-Air Welded Seams and Chemical Resistance

PVC seams weld with hot air similarly to TPO, but the compound itself resists grease, oils, and certain cleaning chemicals better over time. That matters directly at seam locations, which are the failure point when a membrane starts breaking down under chemical exposure. We probe every PVC seam the same way we probe TPO, but we pay particular attention to seams that fall directly under an exhaust discharge path.

Grease film on a membrane surface also affects how new work ties into old work during future repairs, so we clean exposed areas before doing any tie-in weld rather than welding over residue and hoping it holds.

## Standalone Restaurant Roofs Around Shreveport-Bossier

Standalone restaurant buildings usually have a small footprint with a concentrated exhaust load relative to roof area, which makes the grease-exposure problem more intense per square foot than a large kitchen on a big commercial property. We see this on quick-service and full-service restaurant roofs scattered along the retail corridors on both sides of the Red River, and PVC's chemical resistance earns its cost on these smaller, harder-worked roofs even though the total membrane area is modest.

- Exhaust discharge mapping before recommending membrane type or zone coverage
- Grease-resistant PVC membrane specified at concentrated exposure zones
- Seam cleaning and prep before any tie-in weld near exhaust paths
- Fan curb and exhaust penetration flashing detailed individually
- Post-install seam probe focused on high-exposure zones first

## Wind and Hail Performance

PVC handles the same spring storm wind and hail exposure this region sees regularly about as well as TPO does at comparable thickness, so we're not trading storm performance to get the chemical resistance. Fastening pattern still gets engineered to the building's wind zone rather than a generic minimum, and that's true whether the membrane is PVC, TPO, or EPDM.

Hail resistance follows membrane thickness more than membrane chemistry, so a thin PVC sheet isn't automatically tougher against impact than a thicker TPO sheet would be. We'll spec thickness based on the same traffic and exposure analysis regardless of which chemistry the roof needs.

## Budgeting for a Higher Line-Item Membrane

PVC typically costs more than TPO or EPDM per square foot, and we don't pretend otherwise. On a roof without concentrated grease or chemical exposure, that premium doesn't buy anything a cheaper membrane wouldn't already deliver. On a casino back-of-house roof or a restaurant with heavy exhaust load, it buys real service life that a TPO membrane in the same location would burn through faster.

We'll show the reasoning zone by zone if a property has both exposed and unexposed roof areas, because it's common to spec PVC only where the exhaust load actually lands and a standard membrane everywhere else.

## Coordinating With Hood Cleaning Contractors

Commercial kitchen exhaust hoods on casino and restaurant properties get cleaned on a recurring schedule by a separate contractor, and that cleaning cycle interacts directly with the roof around the fan curb. We coordinate with an FM's hood cleaning vendor when we're doing any work near an exhaust fan, because a curb flashing detail that gets disturbed during a hood cleaning service call and then never reported back to facilities is exactly how a small leak starts without anyone connecting it to the right cause.

If your hood cleaning contractor is working near the roof penetration, we'd rather be looped into that schedule than find out after the fact that a curb seal got bumped loose.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About PVC Roofing

### Do we need PVC across the whole roof, or just near the kitchen exhaust?

Usually just the exposed zones. We map exhaust discharge before recommending coverage, and most properties don't need whole-roof PVC unless exhaust sources are spread across the deck.

### How much longer does PVC last under grease exposure compared to TPO?

The gap depends on exhaust volume and cleaning frequency, but PVC consistently outperforms TPO and EPDM under sustained grease contact, which is the entire reason it costs more.

### Does PVC handle Shreveport's hail and wind as well as TPO?

At comparable thickness, yes. Storm performance tracks membrane thickness and fastening pattern more than membrane chemistry.

### Can existing grease-damaged TPO be repaired instead of replaced with PVC?

Sometimes, if the damage is localized and the membrane is otherwise sound. We inspect before recommending a full membrane swap over a targeted repair.

### What maintenance does a PVC roof need near kitchen exhaust?

Periodic cleaning of grease film near discharge points, in addition to standard seam and flashing inspection twice a year.

## Ready to review the roof scope?

[Request a Roof Assessment](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/contact)

# Silicone Roof Coating in Shreveport, LA

> Silicone restoration coating for Shreveport's aging BUR roofs: ponding-water resistance and no tear-off downtime for occupied casinos, hotels, and offices.

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/silicone-roof-coating

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## Silicone Restoration Instead of Tear-Off on Aging Shreveport Roofs

A silicone coating restoration is the option we bring up whenever an aging built-up or modified bitumen roof is structurally sound but tired on the surface, and there's a real budget or downtime reason to avoid a full tear-off. It's the most direct answer to a question we hear constantly from FMs managing older buildings in this market: can we buy more years out of this roof without shutting the building down for a replacement project.

## Ponding Water and Older BUR Slope Problems

A lot of the older built-up roofs across Shreveport's commercial building stock have slope issues that developed over decades, whether from structural settling, added rooftop equipment changing drainage paths, or a design that was marginal from the start. Standing water accelerates membrane breakdown and, over time, that ponding becomes the roof's biggest liability regardless of what membrane sits underneath it.

Silicone coating handles sustained ponding water better than most alternative coating chemistries, which is exactly why it's the right fit for a roof with a known drainage problem that isn't getting fixed this budget cycle. We're honest that the coating manages the symptom; if drainage can be corrected structurally at some point, that's still the better long-term fix.

## No Tear-Off Means No Open Deck Overnight

For a facilities manager, the appeal of a coating restoration goes beyond cost savings; downtime is the bigger factor. A coating project doesn't require opening the deck the way a tear-off does, which means the building stays weathertight every night of the project instead of relying on temporary dry-in protection against an afternoon thunderstorm that showed up ahead of schedule. On an occupied building where tenants are working underneath the roof deck, that's not a minor detail.

We sequence coating work section by section, same as any roofing project, but the risk profile is fundamentally different from a tear-off because there's no exposed substrate at any point in the process.

## What a Roof Needs to Qualify for Coating

Not every aging roof is a coating candidate. We core-cut and inspect for wet insulation, membrane delamination, and structural deck issues before recommending silicone over a full replacement. A roof with trapped moisture under the membrane doesn't get better with a coating on top of it; it gets worse, because the coating traps that moisture in place while masking the symptom from the surface.

- Core cuts across the roof to confirm dry deck and insulation
- Ponding water pattern mapped before recommending coating thickness
- Seam and flashing repair completed before any coating application
- Primer and coating applied per manufacturer mil-thickness requirements
- Post-application inspection for coverage gaps and pinholes

## Weather Windows for Application

Silicone coating needs a dry substrate and adequate cure time before rain hits it, which is a real scheduling constraint in a region where afternoon thunderstorms are a normal part of the summer forecast. We track weather closely during a coating project and stage sections to match realistic dry windows rather than committing a whole roof to a single day's forecast.

Humidity affects cure time too, which we account for when sequencing multiple coating passes rather than assuming a standard cure schedule applies regardless of conditions.

## Extending Service Life Versus Deferring the Inevitable

We're direct with owners about what a coating restoration buys: additional years of service life on a roof that's otherwise sound, not a permanent substitute for eventual replacement. For a building on a five- to ten-year capital horizon, that math often works strongly in favor of coating now and budgeting replacement later, rather than committing full tear-off dollars to a roof that didn't need it yet.

We'll also tell you when coating isn't the answer, particularly if the core cuts come back wet. That's not the conversation anyone wants, but it's the honest one.

## Working Around Occupied Hotel and Casino Buildings

A coating project over a hotel tower or casino annex has a different downtime tolerance than an office building, since guest rooms and gaming floors underneath can't tolerate the same noise or odor exposure a vacant warehouse could absorb without complaint. We schedule coating passes around quiet hours where the building requires it and keep application areas clearly marked so maintenance staff and guests aren't walking through wet coating by accident.

Odor from a curing coating is a real consideration in an occupied hospitality building, and we'll talk through low-odor product options with an FM if guest complaints are a bigger concern than a marginal cost difference.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About Silicone Coating

### How long does a silicone coating restoration extend a roof's service life?

It depends heavily on the condition of the substrate underneath and how well ponding and drainage issues are addressed as part of the project, but it's a meaningful extension when the roof qualifies.

### Can we coat a roof that already has some ponding water?

Yes, silicone is specifically suited to standing water exposure, which is one of the main reasons it's chosen over alternative coating chemistries in this market.

### What disqualifies a roof from coating restoration?

Wet insulation, significant membrane delamination, or structural deck problems found during core-cut inspection. Coating over trapped moisture makes the underlying problem worse, not better.

### Does coating work interrupt building operations the way a tear-off would?

No, that's the main advantage. There's no open deck at any point, so the building stays weathertight overnight throughout the project.

### How often does a coated roof need recoating after the first application?

That depends on coating thickness, UV exposure, and foot traffic, which is why we build periodic inspection into the maintenance plan rather than assuming a fixed recoat interval.

## Ready to review the roof scope?

[Request a Roof Assessment](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/contact)

# Spray Polyurethane Foam Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> Spray foam roofing for Shreveport's older industrial and municipal buildings: continuous coverage over irregular decks and added insulation value

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/spray-polyurethane-foam

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## Spray Foam for Irregular Rooflines and Retrofit Insulation Gaps

Spray polyurethane foam is the system we bring up when a roof deck has more going on than a flat, uniform field: penetrations clustered unevenly, old mechanical curbs from equipment that's since been removed, or a roofline that was added onto in pieces over decades. Older industrial and municipal buildings around Shreveport tend to have exactly that kind of deck, and foam's ability to conform to irregular geometry solves problems a sheet membrane can't without extensive custom flashing.

## Continuous Coverage Around Obstacles

Spray-applied foam self-levels and conforms around curbs, pipe clusters, and odd transitions in a way that a rolled membrane physically can't without a lot of hand-cut detail work. On a municipal building or older plant with decades of accumulated rooftop penetrations, that continuous coverage reduces the number of individual flashing details a crew has to build correctly, which is also fewer places for a future leak to start.

We still detail every penetration properly rather than assuming the foam alone solves the transition, but the base coverage gives us a better starting point on a complicated deck than a sheet membrane would.

## Adding R-Value to Buildings That Never Had It

A lot of older commercial and industrial buildings in this market were built with minimal or no roof insulation, because energy codes at the time didn't require it and utility costs weren't the driver they are now. Spray foam adds real insulation value directly at the roof deck during the same project that addresses waterproofing, which is a meaningfully different value proposition than a membrane-only recover that leaves the building's insulation gap exactly where it was.

For a building on a tight capital budget where a separate insulation retrofit project was never going to get funded on its own, bundling that improvement into the roofing project is often the only realistic way it happens.

## Humidity and Dew Point During Application

Foam application is unforgiving about substrate moisture and dew point conditions in a way that some other systems aren't. Spraying foam onto a damp deck, or in conditions where dew point is close to substrate temperature, traps moisture and creates adhesion problems that don't show up until later. Ark-La-Tex humidity makes this a real scheduling constraint, not a theoretical one, and we hold application when conditions aren't right rather than pushing through to keep a schedule.

- Deck moisture and dew point check before any foam application begins
- Substrate cleaning and prep at every existing penetration and curb
- Foam thickness applied to specified R-value target across the field
- Protective coating applied over foam per manufacturer requirements
- Post-application inspection for coverage consistency and pinholes

## Protective Coating and UV Exposure

Foam itself isn't UV-stable and needs a protective coating over it, typically silicone or acrylic, applied at a specified thickness. That coating is what actually takes the sun exposure over the life of the roof, and it needs periodic recoating on a schedule tied to UV exposure and foot traffic rather than a one-time application that's expected to last the life of the roof.

We build that recoating interval into the maintenance conversation up front, because a foam roof that isn't recoated on schedule loses its protective layer well before the foam substrate itself would otherwise need replacement.

## Where Foam Isn't the Right Answer

Foam isn't the default recommendation for a straightforward flat roof without unusual geometry or insulation gaps. On a building where a standard single-ply membrane solves the problem at lower cost and simpler long-term maintenance, we'll say so rather than pushing foam because it's a more involved, higher-margin project. Foam earns its place specifically on the complicated decks and insulation-poor buildings where it solves problems other systems can't.

We also flag foam as a poor fit on roofs with heavy foot traffic or storage, since the protective coating takes more wear in those conditions than it does on a low-traffic industrial roof.

## Foam Projects on Municipal and Public-Building Budgets

Municipal buildings and public facilities in this area typically move through a bond or budget-approval cycle before a roofing project gets funded, which is a slower process than a private owner deciding to move forward on a proposal. We build project timelines around that reality, including phased foam application across fiscal years when a full-building project doesn't fit one year's approved budget.

We'll also provide the documentation a public procurement process usually requires, including itemized scope and specified R-value targets, so the project can move through approval without a facilities director having to translate our recommendation into whatever format the finance office needs.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About Spray Foam Roofing

### Does spray foam work on any roof, or only irregular ones?

It works on any roof, but it earns its cost specifically on decks with complex geometry, accumulated penetrations, or missing insulation. On a simple flat roof, a membrane system is often the more cost-effective choice.

### How much does foam actually add in R-value?

That depends on the applied thickness, which we spec to a target R-value based on the building's current insulation gap and budget.

### Can foam be applied in Shreveport's summer humidity?

Only within the right dew point and substrate moisture window. We monitor conditions closely and hold application rather than spraying onto a damp or borderline deck.

### How often does the protective coating need reapplication?

It depends on UV exposure and foot traffic, but we build a recoating interval into the maintenance plan rather than treating the first coating as a lifetime application.

### Is foam roofing more expensive than a membrane recover?

Often comparable or higher upfront, but on a building with real insulation gaps, it's addressing two problems in one project rather than one, which changes the value comparison.

## Ready to review the roof scope?

[Request a Roof Assessment](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/contact)

# 60-Mil TPO Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> 60-mil TPO for Shreveport strip retail and standalone restaurants: weld-window discipline in Ark-La-Tex humidity and fastening for spring thunderstorm wind

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/tpo-60-mil

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## 60-Mil TPO for Shreveport's Lighter-Traffic Roof Assets

Sixty-mil TPO is the membrane we spec most often for retail strips, standalone restaurants, and smaller office buildings along Youree Drive and out toward Bossier City. It's a budget-tier single-ply sheet, and for a roof that only sees an HVAC tech twice a year, that's the right call. If your roof asset gets regular foot traffic or rooftop storage, we'll say so before you sign anything, because that's where 60-mil starts to look thin.

## Matching Membrane Thickness to the Work Order History

Before we quote a thickness, we ask what the work order log actually says about this roof. A building with two service calls a year for a rooftop package unit doesn't need the same puncture resistance as a plant with a maintenance crew walking the deck weekly. Sixty-mil TPO holds up fine under that lighter load, and paying for 80-mil coverage you'll never use just inflates the capital request without buying anything back in service life.

Where we push back is when a tenant starts using the roof as storage, or a new rooftop unit gets added mid-lease without anyone re-evaluating the membrane spec. That's a conversation we'd rather have before the work order, not after a puncture claim.

## Weld Windows in Ark-La-Tex Humidity

Hot-air welding TPO seams depends on a dry membrane surface, and Shreveport's humidity doesn't always cooperate, especially in the shoulder months when morning dew sits on the deck longer than crews expect. We schedule weld work around that, not around the clock, because a seam welded over a damp surface is a seam that fails quietly, usually the following summer when nobody's watching for it.

Every seam gets probed before the crew leaves the roof. On a 60-mil job over a smaller building that's a same-day process, and we log the results the same day rather than filing them from memory later.

## Spring Storm Wind and Fastening Discipline

Shreveport sits inside a corridor that takes fast-moving spring squall lines seriously, and the wind that comes ahead of those lines is where a marginal fastening pattern gets exposed at the parapet edge first. We fasten every 60-mil install to the wind zone the building actually sits in rather than a generic minimum, because that's the difference between a membrane that's still on the roof after the next line of storms and one that isn't.

- Deck condition check and fastener pull-out testing before membrane goes down
- Tighter fastening at perimeter and corner zones than the field of the roof
- Coping and termination bar detail checked at every parapet run
- Every penetration and curb flashed and photographed individually
- Seam probe results recorded on the day of install, not reconstructed later

## What Goes in the File Before We Leave

A good share of our work eventually intersects an insurance claim somewhere in the roof's life, whether that's hail, straight-line wind, or a tenant's rooftop unit failure. We photograph deck conditions before membrane, log fastener patterns, and keep flashing detail shots on file, because that paperwork is what turns a disputed claim into a routine one when an adjuster shows up years later.

We don't promise a claim outcome and we won't tell you the install guarantees anything about a future adjuster's decision. What we can control is whether the roof's own history gives that adjuster a reason to question the claim. Usually it's a short file. We keep it anyway.

## Budget Planning Around a 60-Mil Roof Asset

For an FM managing a roof asset on a capital plan rather than reacting to leaks, 60-mil TPO is easy to plan around. It's a known cost, a known install timeline, and a membrane that doesn't ask for special handling once it's down. We'll tell you honestly where it sits in a multi-building portfolio next to heavier-traffic assets that need the 80-mil spec instead.

If downtime matters more than upfront cost on a particular building, we'll walk through install sequencing that keeps sections of the roof dry each night rather than opening the whole deck at once. That's a scheduling conversation worth having before the crew mobilizes.

## Sequencing a Multi-Building Re-Roof Around One Crew

A property manager holding several small retail pads or restaurant buildings across the Youree Drive corridor and out toward Bossier City rarely has budget to re-roof all of them in one fiscal year. We build a phased schedule instead: two or three buildings this cycle, the rest queued for the following year, with the same crew and membrane spec carried across every phase so warranty paperwork and maintenance records stay consistent across the portfolio.

That consistency matters more than it sounds like it should. When every building in a portfolio has the same 60-mil TPO spec, the same fastening standard, and the same inspection interval, a facilities team can manage the whole group off one maintenance calendar instead of tracking a different system for every address.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About 60-Mil TPO

### Is 60-mil too thin for a Shreveport roof?

Not for the buildings it's meant for. On a roof with light, occasional traffic, 60-mil TPO holds up through a normal service life. The mistake is specifying it on a roof that gets regular foot traffic or storage, where the extra mils of an 80-mil sheet actually earn their cost.

### How does humidity affect the install timeline?

It can push weld work later in the morning or stop it altogether on a heavy dew day. We build that into the schedule up front rather than treating it as a delay, since forcing a weld over a damp deck creates problems that show up months later.

### Does 60-mil TPO need a different maintenance plan than 80-mil?

Not fundamentally. Both need the same twice-yearly inspection rhythm. The difference is how much margin the membrane has if maintenance slips for a season, and 60-mil has less of it.

### Can we recoat a 60-mil roof instead of replacing it later?

Often, yes, if the membrane is still sound and just losing reflectivity or picking up minor seam wear. We evaluate that case by case rather than defaulting to a silicone recoat automatically.

### What happens if a new rooftop unit gets added after install?

Any new curb or penetration needs to be flashed and documented the same way the original install was. Loop us in before a mechanical contractor cuts into the membrane, not after, and it stays a five-minute site visit instead of a warranty dispute.

# 80-Mil TPO Roofing in Shreveport, LA

> 80-mil TPO for Shreveport manufacturing plants and casino back-of-house roofs: hail resistance, dock traffic, and rooftop mechanical yard durability

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems/tpo-80-mil

[All Roof Systems](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/roof-systems)

## 80-Mil TPO for Roofs That Take Real Rooftop Traffic

Eighty-mil TPO is the heavier of the two thicknesses we install, and it earns its higher line-item cost on buildings where the roof deck functions as a working surface rather than a passive lid. Manufacturing plants along the I-20 corridor, distribution buildings, and casino back-of-house rooftop mechanical yards in Bossier City all fall into that category. The extra mils buy puncture resistance for foot traffic, ladder work, and rooftop equipment servicing that a 60-mil sheet wasn't built to absorb.

## Reading a Roof's Traffic Profile Before Specifying Thickness

We walk the deck before quoting membrane thickness, and we're looking for specific signs: worn paths between rooftop units, ladder scuffing near access hatches, tool marks near mechanical curbs. On a plant roof serving heavy HVAC and process equipment, that traffic pattern is constant, and it's the same reasoning that pushes us toward 80-mil on casino properties where the back-of-house kitchen exhaust fans, chillers, and generator equipment all sit on the same deck a maintenance crew is walking multiple times a week.

If a building doesn't show that traffic pattern, we'll say the 60-mil sheet is the more defensible spend. Overspecifying membrane thickness on a low-traffic roof doesn't buy service life; it just moves budget away from a building that actually needs it.

## Hail Resistance and Ark-La-Tex Storm Cells

This part of Louisiana takes hail seriously, usually from the same spring convective cells that bring the straight-line wind. Eighty-mil TPO's added thickness gives a meaningfully better puncture-resistance margin against hail impact than the 60-mil sheet, which matters on a plant roof where a compromised membrane means water finding its way to process equipment below rather than only an office ceiling tile.

We document hail exposure the same way we document install quality: photos of any impact marks, dated, tied to storm events where we can confirm them against weather records rather than assuming every dimple in the membrane is storm-related.

## Rooftop Mechanical Yards and Dock Traffic

A distribution building's roof usually has more rooftop mechanical equipment per square foot than the building footprint suggests, and every one of those units needs a curb, a flashing detail, and periodic technician access. Eighty-mil TPO holds up to that access pattern better over the membrane's service life, particularly around curbs where techs set tools and parts down without thinking about what's underneath them.

- Traffic-pattern walk of the existing or planned rooftop equipment layout
- Membrane thickness matched to actual foot-traffic and ladder-access frequency
- Reinforced walkway pads at primary access routes between units
- Curb and equipment-pad flashing detailed for repeat technician access
- Post-install seam probe with hail-exposure baseline photos on file

## Welding in Summer Heat and Humidity

Deck surface temperatures on a dark substrate climb fast once the Louisiana sun is on it, and that changes how the membrane handles under the hot-air welder well before ambient air temperature would suggest a problem. We shift welding to early mornings on 80-mil tear-offs and re-covers specifically because afternoon deck temperatures make weld consistency harder to hold across a large plant or distribution roof.

Every seam gets probed before the crew signs off, and on a larger 80-mil roof that's a multi-day process broken into completed sections rather than one pass at the end of the job.

## Budget Conversations for Heavy-Use Roof Assets

For an FM managing capital across several buildings, 80-mil TPO is usually the higher line item in the portfolio, and it should be. We'll walk through why a specific building justifies it rather than asking you to take our word for a blanket recommendation. If a roof's traffic profile doesn't support the extra cost, we'll tell you that too.

We also build the maintenance plan around the traffic pattern once the membrane is down, because a heavy-use roof needs more frequent walkway inspection than a low-traffic one, even with the thicker sheet installed.

## Coordinating Roof Access With Casino and Plant Operations

A casino property in Bossier City doesn't stop running while a roof crew is working overhead, and a manufacturing plant on a production schedule doesn't shut a line down for a re-roof either. We plan access routes, staging areas, and material hoisting around whatever operation is happening below, and we coordinate noise-generating work like tear-off demolition with the building's own schedule rather than assuming the roof is ours to run however's convenient for the crew.

On a casino back-of-house roof specifically, that means working around kitchen service hours and keeping exhaust equipment functional throughout the project, since taking a commercial kitchen's ventilation offline mid-shift isn't something either of us wants to explain to the health inspector.

## Questions Facilities Managers Ask About 80-Mil TPO

### Is 80-mil overkill for a mid-size office building?

Usually, yes, unless that building has unusually heavy rooftop mechanical traffic. We'd rather steer that budget toward the 60-mil sheet and put the difference toward a building that actually needs the heavier membrane.

### Does 80-mil TPO cost meaningfully more to install?

The material cost is higher and welding takes marginally longer per linear foot of seam, but on a heavy-traffic roof the added service life and reduced puncture-repair calls usually justify it over the ownership period.

### How much hail does 80-mil TPO actually resist?

No membrane is hail-proof, but 80-mil's added thickness gives a real margin over 60-mil against smaller to moderate hail. Large hail can still compromise any single-ply membrane, which is why post-storm inspection matters regardless of thickness.

### Can 80-mil TPO go over an existing roof without a full tear-off?

Sometimes, if the existing deck and insulation are dry and sound. We evaluate that with a core cut before recommending a recover over a full replacement.

### What maintenance schedule fits an 80-mil roof with heavy equipment traffic?

We'd recommend inspection at least twice a year, plus a walkway-pad check any time new rooftop equipment gets added or a maintenance contractor changes.

## Ready to review the roof scope?

# Commercial Roofing Contractors Barksdale Afb Area, LA

> Commercial roofing contractors serving Barksdale Afb Area, LA with commercial roof repair, replacement, coatings, maintenance programs and inspections.

Canonical: https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/service-areas/barksdale-afb-area

[All Service Areas](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/service-areas)

## Commercial Roofers in Barksdale Afb Area

For commercial properties in Barksdale Afb Area, the defensible choice between repair, restoration, and replacement starts with roof-system condition, moisture findings, drainage performance, and remaining service life. Barksdale is home to Air Force Global Strike Command and the 2nd Bomb Wing, and that mission pulls a whole layer of support buildings around it: defense contractor offices, logistics and warehouse space, and vendor facilities that exist because the base exists. None of that work looks like a typical commercial roof job, mostly because of who has to sign off on when a crew shows up.

## Security Clearance Changes the Schedule Before the Scope Does

A building supporting Global Strike Command operations, even a leased office a mile off base, often runs under access rules that a standard commercial tenant never deals with. Escort requirements, badge verification, and restricted areas inside a facility can turn a routine roof inspection into a coordination exercise before a single ladder goes up.

We plan around that from the first phone call. If a property manager tells us a section of roof sits over a controlled space, we build the access plan, the crew list, and the timeline around that constraint instead of finding out about it on inspection day.

## Logistics and Warehouse Buildings Serving the Base

A good share of the commercial building stock in this area is logistics and warehouse space, staging ground for contractors moving parts, equipment, and supplies in and out of the base. These roofs are typically TPO or another single-ply membrane over metal deck, sized for a specific drainage tributary that changes the moment a tenant adds rooftop equipment or reconfigures interior racking.

We check that the original drain and scupper layout still matches current roof loading before recommending anything, because a warehouse that's had three tenants and two equipment upgrades since it was built rarely still drains the way the original design intended.

## Contractor Office Buildings and Standing Seam Roofs

Newer contractor and vendor office buildings in the area lean toward standing seam metal roofing, valued for its long service life and lower long-term maintenance burden compared to older built-up systems. We handle [standing seam metal roofing](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/standing-seam-metal-roofing) installation and repair with the same attention to fastener concealment and thermal movement that any metal system demands, whether the building is a straightforward office or something with tighter access controls.

## What We Check On a Base-Adjacent Roof

- Drainage tributary areas that no longer match current rooftop equipment loads
- Fastener backout or panel movement on standing seam roofs from thermal cycling
- Membrane punctures near HVAC clusters on office and lab buildings
- Flashing failures at loading dock canopies on logistics buildings
- Sealant failure at penetrations added after original construction
- Ponding at low points on older warehouse roofs

## Weather Stress on Flat and Low-Slope Roofs Here

Ark-La-Tex humidity works on membranes year-round, and this area sees its share of spring severe weather and hail that can go unnoticed on a large warehouse roof until a tenant reports a leak weeks later. Occasional winter ice events add another layer of stress on flashing and rooftop equipment enclosures that aren't built for glaze ice.

When storm damage hits a facility supporting base operations, we document conditions and write scope the same way we would anywhere else, factually and without promising a specific claim outcome, because a defense contractor's insurance and compliance requirements are usually stricter than a typical commercial policy.

## Preventive Maintenance Reduces Emergency Calls Near a Restricted Site

An emergency roof call at a facility with restricted access takes longer to resolve than the same call at an open commercial building, simply because getting a crew cleared and escorted onto the roof adds a step that a standard office building never requires. That makes routine, scheduled maintenance worth more here than almost anywhere else in the metro.

A standing [preventive maintenance program](https://commercialroofersshreveport.com/services/preventive-maintenance-programs) lets us catch a lifted seam or a clogged drain during a pre-cleared, scheduled visit instead of during an emergency access request after hours, which matters when every unplanned visit to a base-adjacent facility means extra coordination on both ends.

We also keep a longer paper trail on these properties than we would elsewhere, because a facilities manager supporting a defense contract often needs to show an auditor or a prime contractor that roof conditions were tracked and addressed on schedule, not discovered during a crisis.

## Questions From Facilities Managers in This Area

### Do you need a security clearance to work on buildings near the base?

We don't hold clearances ourselves, but we coordinate with whatever escort or access process the property or its tenant requires, and we plan crew schedules around that rather than treating it as an afterthought.

### How do you handle roof access on a building with restricted interior areas?

We identify which roof sections sit over controlled space before scheduling, then route crew movement and material staging to avoid those areas or work under whatever escort protocol is required.

### Why do so many newer buildings here use standing seam metal instead of single-ply?

Standing seam holds up well against long-term maintenance costs and has a strong service life record, which matters to contractor and vendor tenants who don't want a roof decision revisited every few years.

### What's the most common roofing problem on the logistics buildings out here?

Drainage mismatches. Buildings get new tenants, new equipment, and reconfigured interiors over the years, and the roof's original drainage design often stops matching what's actually happening up there.

### Can you inspect a roof without disrupting operations inside a secure facility?

Generally yes. We schedule around whatever escort and access requirements exist and keep the inspection footprint as small and quiet as the facility needs it to be.
